newsitem.title: UK: By-election win boosts UK Conservatives' morale.
newsitem.headline: By-election win boosts UK Conservatives' morale.

text.p: Britain's ruling Labour party failed on Friday its first test with voters since it took power when the Conservatives retained the parliamentary seat of Uxbridge, west London, in a by-election.

Conservative John Randall, a local furniture shop owner, won his party's first by-election since 1989 by defeating Labour's Andy Slaughter by a margin of 3,766 votes -- five times its majority of 724 at the May 1 general election.

Conservatives hailed the result as a victory for their young new leader, William Hague, who replaced ex-prime minister John Major after Labour's landslide victory at the general election ended 18 years of Conservative rule.
"You've seen the beginning of our recovery," said Sir Norman Fowler, the Conservatives' environment spokesman, on BBC television.
"That is the political significance of this by-election and I think that you've also seen the ending, the stopping, of the Labour bandwagon. So this is a very important by-election result."
The result will make no difference in the House of Commons, which broke up on Thursday for a three-month holiday. Labour has a commanding majority of 178 in the 659-seat lower chamber.
Labour, which has won high approval ratings for the raft of policies it has energetically launched in its three months in office, put a brave face on the defeat.
Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott said Uxbridge was a traditional Conservative stronghold and it would have been a shock if Labour had captured it.

"As far as I'm concerned, it was a safe Tory seat. They've now held on to it. We've kept our proportion of the vote...We'll get on now with convincing the electorate in this country they were right to vote for us," Prescott said.
A MORI opinion poll on Thursday gave Labour a national 34-point lead over the Conservatives at 57 to 23 percent, but party officials had played down expectations of a victory at Uxbridge.

BBC political expert Bill Bush said Labour was probably damaged by a row over its selection of Slaughter, leader of a inner London local authority, instead of a local candidate. One local Labour councillor resigned from the party over the row.
Nevertheless, Bush said the Conservatives had reason to be pleased.

"It's clearly better than anything the national opinion polls have suggested over the past few weeks," he said. "It's a very good performance. I'm sure that there'll be some head scratching in Labour circles."
